analysis.one_liner: Bans piece-rate pay for garment workers and makes brands liable for wage theft in their supply chains.
analysis.headline: The FABRIC Act, which would have required garment workers to be paid an hourly minimum wage and made fashion brands liable for wage violations in their supply chains, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2022, drew 6 cosponsors, and died without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The FABRIC Act would have ended piece-rate pay — paying garment workers per item sewn instead of by the hour — and guaranteed them at least the federal hourly minimum wage. It would have made fashion brands financially liable when the factories they hire cheat workers out of wages, and required garment manufacturers and contractors to register annually with the Department of Labor. It also offered a 30% tax credit and federal grants to companies that move garment production back to the United States.
analysis.who_benefits: Garment workers — disproportionately immigrant women in places like Los Angeles — who are frequently paid by the piece at rates that fall below minimum wage and sometimes go unpaid entirely. The bill guarantees them an hourly wage, allows incentive bonuses on top, and gives them someone to collect from when a contractor goes broke or vanishes: the brand, which shares joint and several liability for wage violations. Domestic garment manufacturers and nonprofits would also benefit from up to $5 million in federal grants per entity, a new federal Garment Industry office, and a 30% tax credit for relocating production to the US, with priority going to unionized shops and minority-, women-, and veteran-owned businesses.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits paying garment workers by the piece or unit and requires an hourly wage of at least the federal minimum under the Fair Labor Standards Act, while still allowing incentive bonuses on top of hourly pay.

Makes 'brand guarantors' — the fashion companies and licensors that contract for garment manufacturing — jointly and severally liable for wage violations by the factories and subcontractors they hire, so workers can recover unpaid wages from the brand rather than only from a shuttered contractor.

Requires every garment manufacturer and contractor to register annually with the Department of Labor, verify workers' compensation coverage, disclose wage-law violations by owners and major shareholders over the prior three years, and post their registration certificate where workers can see it — with civil penalties up to $50,000,000 for violations.

Creates a Department of Labor Office of the Garment Industry with an Undersecretary to run enforcement and a $40 million grant program supporting domestic garment manufacturing, with priority for unionized workforces and minority-, women-, and veteran-owned businesses.

Adds a 30% tax credit for the cost of moving garment business units from overseas back to HUBZones or low-income communities in the United States, conditioned on increasing total full-time-equivalent employment.

analysis.who_pays: Garment manufacturers and contractors, who would have to pay hourly wages instead of piece rates, register annually at $200 per registration, verify workers' compensation insurance, and face penalties up to $50 million. Fashion brands and licensors would bear new financial liability for wage violations anywhere in their contracting chains. Taxpayers would fund the new federal office ($10 million plus $3 million per year) and grant program ($40 million authorized), and the Treasury would lose revenue from the 30% insourcing tax credit.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls hardest on small contractors. Annual registration requires the names, addresses, and Social Security numbers of every production employee and every owner, officer, and major shareholder, plus a $200 fee and workers' compensation verification — paperwork that could push marginal shops out of business rather than into compliance.

Ending piece rate could cut legitimate earnings: fast, productive sewers who currently out-earn the hourly minimum by working quickly would be capped at hourly pay, and while the bill allows incentive bonuses it leaves their design to employers and regulators.

Joint and several liability exposes brands to litigation over factory conduct they may not directly control, although the bill includes an affirmative defense for a brand that shows it had no knowledge of a violation.

The insourcing tax credit and grants direct federal money to private manufacturers, and the credit's relocation-incentive design invites tax planning — companies could restructure units to claim the 30% credit on costs they would have incurred anyway.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core wage protections address a well-documented problem: piece-rate pay in the garment sector is the mechanism behind sub-minimum and unpaid wages, and brand liability attacks the subcontracting structure that lets wage theft happen without consequences for the companies profiting from it. Those gains are real but narrow — the US garment workforce is small. The costs fall on the employers causing the problem, which is the point, though small compliant shops share the paperwork burden. The reshoring tax credit and grants are a costlier and less targeted addition, and the bill never received any committee review, so no cost estimates or refined design were ever produced.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2022 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the FABRIC Act on May 12, 2022, joined at introduction by Senators Booker, Warren, and Sanders.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over the bill's tax provisions and wage law.
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote; its only cosponsors were 5 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents, for 6 in total.
When the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, the bill died, as all legislation does that has not passed both chambers by the end of a Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Garment manufacturers, contractors, and the brands that hire them are better off: they avoided hourly wage mandates, joint liability for supply-chain wage theft, annual registration, and penalties up to $50 million. Garment workers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no vote split exists; all 6 cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Sanders, and no Republican supported it.

industries.note: The bill would have ended piece-rate pay — the primary mechanism for sub-minimum wages in the sector — and imposed annual registration, disclosure of wage-law violations, and penalties up to $50 million. Its interest in the bill ran directly against the workers it pays.

Brands that contract for garment manufacturing would have become jointly and severally liable for wage violations by the factories and subcontractors they hire, ending the practice of profiting from low bids while leaving wage theft with the contractor. They would also have qualified for the 30% insourcing credit if they moved production to the US.

Compliant domestic producers would have gained a $40 million grant program, a dedicated federal office, and a 30% tax credit for relocating production from abroad to HUBZones and low-income communities, with priority for unionized and minority-, women-, and veteran-owned shops.
